event.through: The AI goes in through the poem itself, in Samuel Butler's prose translation of 1900. Butler calls him Ulysses and the goddess Minerva; the story is the same.

fragments.text: Nausicaa
Went down to the washing-pools with her maids, and found a shipwrecked man hiding in the bushes.
Told the stranger to follow her cart only as far as the city walls, so that people wouldn't talk.
Played ball with her maids on the shore while the washing dried.
Asked her father for the mule cart to go washing, too shy to mention marriage. He understood anyway.
Arete
Noticed that the stranger was wearing clothes she had made, and asked him who he was.
Is the one Nausicaa told the stranger to kneel to first, before the king.
Is honoured by her people as few women are, and settles their quarrels.
Wants the stranger to stay one more night, so the gifts can all be gathered.
Demodocus
Sang of the quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles, and the stranger hid his face in his cloak and wept.
Was asked by the stranger for the song of the wooden horse, and sang it.
The Muse took away his sight, and gave him sweet song in its place.
The herald hangs his lyre on a peg above his head, and guides his hand to it.
Euryalus
Mocked the stranger for looking more like a merchant than an athlete.
Gave the stranger a bronze sword with a silver hilt, to make amends.
Won the wrestling at the games.
Was told by the king to apologise, with words and a gift.
Alcinous
Asked the stranger at last to tell them his name, his country, and why he wept at the songs.
Promised the stranger a ship home. Phaeacian ships need no helmsman: they know where men mean to go.
Has an orchard where pears, apples and figs ripen all year round.
Remembers a prophecy that Poseidon would one day punish them for carrying strangers home.
Elpenor
Slept on Circe's roof after too much wine, forgot the ladder when he woke, and fell.
Was the first of the dead to speak to Odysseus, and asked to be buried with his oar.
Was not much of a fighter, the poem says, and not very clever.
Lay unburied on Circe's island while the others hurried to the ships.
Polites
Heard someone singing at a loom inside Circe's house, and urged the others to call out.
Was among the men Circe turned into pigs, though their minds stayed their own.
Is the man Odysseus calls the dearest and most trusted of his crew.
Was given cheese, barley and honey in wine by Circe, with her drug in it.
Eurylochus
Would not go into Circe's house, and ran back alone to tell what had happened.
Talked the starving crew into killing the Sun-god's cattle.
Warns that Odysseus will lead them all to ruin, as he did in the Cyclops's cave.
Waited out a month of contrary winds on the Sun-god's island.
A rower of Ithaca
Rowed past the Sirens with beeswax in his ears, and never heard a note.
Was one of the men who opened the bag of winds while their captain slept.
Ate the lotus, and wept when he was dragged back to the ship.
The winds from the bag blew them all the way back to Aeolus's island.
Feasted on the Cyclops's sheep on the shore, after the escape.
Six of his shipmates were taken by Scylla as they passed.
Anticlea
Came to her son among the dead, and did not know him until she had drunk the blood.
Told her son that she died of missing him.
Three times he tried to hold her, and three times she passed through his arms like a shadow.
Told him Penelope still waited for him, and Telemachus still kept his lands.

ranks.look: [DRAFT] In the hall of Alcinous, {listeners:listener waits:listeners wait}. The story will begin in Ithaca, where suitors eat his cattle in his own hall and his son watches.
ranks.story: [DRAFT] The poem begins not with him but with his son. Telemachus sits among the suitors eating his father's cattle, and a stranger at the door turns out to be a goddess.

teaches.text: The Odyssey opens with Telemachus, not Odysseus. For its first four books Odysseus is only talked about, while his son sails to Pylos and Sparta for news of him.
teaches.title: It starts with his son

ranks.title: Ithaca without him

ranks.look: [DRAFT] {listeners:listener leans:listeners lean} in as the tale reaches Calypso's island: seven years on a shore, looking at the sea.
ranks.story: [DRAFT] Seven years on an island with a goddess who offers to make him immortal. He sits on the shore each day and looks at the sea. Hermes brings the order to let him go, and he builds a raft.

teaches.text: We first meet Odysseus himself in Book 5, weeping on Calypso's shore. She offers him a life that never ends, and he chooses home, and Penelope, instead.
teaches.title: Where we meet him

ranks.title: Calypso's island

ranks.look: [DRAFT] Golden youths hold torches over the feast. {listeners:listener leans:listeners lean} in, {songs:song has:songs have} been sung, and the stranger has said his name.
ranks.story: [DRAFT] In the hall of Alcinous the stranger says his name at last, and tells it all: the Cyclops, the bag of winds, Circe, the dead, the Sirens. By the end of his telling, every man who sailed with him is lost.

teaches.text: The famous adventures, the Cyclops, Circe and the Sirens, are told by Odysseus himself, at a feast, in Books 9 to 12. The poem lets its hero narrate his own legend, to people who have no way to check it.
teaches.title: He tells it himself

ranks.title: The telling

ranks.look: [DRAFT] {songs:song:songs} sung, and the Phaeacian ship has gone. On Ithaca an old beggar sits by the swineherd's fire, and a dog lifts its head.
ranks.story: [DRAFT] Home, but as a beggar. The swineherd Eumaeus feeds him without knowing him. At the palace an old dog, lying neglected on a dung heap, knows him at once, lowers his ears, and dies.

teaches.text: Athena disguises Odysseus as an old beggar, and he is recognised one by one. The first to know him is not a person but his old dog Argos, who has waited twenty years.
teaches.title: Argos

ranks.title: Home in disguise

ranks.look: [DRAFT] {feasts:feast:feasts} laid in the hall. The old bow comes down from the storeroom, and twelve axes stand in a line.
ranks.story: [DRAFT] Only he can string the old bow. And when it is over, Penelope tests him not with the bow but with their bed: one post of it is a living olive tree, and only the two of them know.

teaches.text: Penelope sets the suitors the contest of the bow. Afterwards she tests the stranger herself, asking for their bed to be moved; he protests that it can't be, because he built it around an olive tree.
teaches.title: The bed

ranks.title: The bow and the bed

butler-odyssey.author: Homer, translated by Samuel Butler
butler-odyssey.note: Prose translation, public domain. Cite by book ("Book 12"). Butler uses Latin names for the gods and for Odysseus (Ulysses, Minerva, Jove); the game says Odysseus and Athena, and quotes nothing longer than a phrase.
butler-odyssey.title: The Odyssey

pages.text: [DRAFT] He took in an old beggar, fed him, and listened to his long, made-up story, without knowing it was his own master.
pages.title: The swineherd's hut

pages.text: [DRAFT] He was born a king's son on a far island, stolen as a child by Phoenician traders, and sold to Laertes.
pages.title: His own story

pages.text: [DRAFT] Shown the old scar, he knew his master, and wept.
pages.title: The scar

pages.text: [DRAFT] He fought beside Odysseus and Telemachus in the hall.
pages.title: Beside him

pages.text: [DRAFT] He sang for the suitors in Odysseus's hall because they made him. His song was the sad homecoming of the Greeks from Troy.
pages.title: Singing for the suitors

pages.text: [DRAFT] Penelope came down and asked him to sing something else. Telemachus said a bard should sing what moves him.
pages.title: Penelope's tears

pages.text: [DRAFT] When the fighting came, he clasped Odysseus's knees and begged; Telemachus said he had sung under force, and he was spared.
pages.title: Spared

pages.text: [DRAFT] He said no one taught him: a god put every kind of song into his heart.
pages.title: Self-taught

pages.text: [DRAFT] He overheard the suitors plotting to ambush Telemachus at sea, and told Penelope.
pages.title: Overheard

pages.text: [DRAFT] He served the suitors' feasts and kept faith with the household all the same.
pages.title: In the hall

pages.text: [DRAFT] In the fight he hid under a chair wrapped in a fresh oxhide, and Telemachus asked that he be spared.
pages.title: Under the chair

pages.text: [DRAFT] He told the angry Ithacans that he had seen a god standing beside Odysseus.
pages.title: For peace

pages.text: [DRAFT] He brought a heifer across from the mainland for the suitors' feast, and greeted the ragged beggar kindly.
pages.title: The cowherd

pages.text: [DRAFT] Seeing the beggar, he thought of his master, perhaps wandering in rags somewhere too, and his eyes filled.
pages.title: Missing him

pages.text: [DRAFT] He was shown the scar with Eumaeus, and both men wept.
pages.title: The scar

pages.text: [DRAFT] He barred the courtyard gates, so no one could leave once the bow was strung.
pages.title: The gate

pages.text: [DRAFT] At the king's word he mixed wine for the guests, so they could pour it for the gods.
pages.title: Mixing the wine

pages.text: [DRAFT] He set a chair for Demodocus against a pillar, and hung the lyre where he could reach it.
pages.title: The bard's chair

pages.text: [DRAFT] He took the bard by the hand and led him out to the games.
pages.title: Leading him out
